1.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:16.

2.note: See how you translated **son of man** in [2:1](ta:02).
See how you translated a similar phrase in Ezekiel 26:17. Alternate translation: [sing a mourning song for Tyre]

3.q: ה⁠ישבתי עַל מְבוֹאֹ֣ת יָ֔ם רֹכֶ֨לֶת֙ הָֽ⁠עַמִּ֔ים אֶל אִיִּ֖ים רַבִּ֑ים
3.note: Yahweh is speaking of **Tyre** as if it were a person who could live by the sea and trade with other peoples. He means the city of Tyre and the people who lived and traded there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the city at the entrances of the sea, whose people traded with the peoples of many coastlands]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the harbors of Tyre were **entrances** or doorways through which ships came in from **the sea**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at the harbors where ships come in from the sea]

Here, **many coastlands** represents “the people who live in many lands along the coast.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the inhabitants of many lands along the coast]

3.q: כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֔ה צ֕וֹר אַ֣תְּ אָמַ֔רְתְּ אֲנִ֖י כְּלִ֥ילַת יֹֽפִי
3.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [thus says the Lord Yahweh, ‘Tyre, you, you have said that you are perfect of beauty.]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **have said** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it was Tyre itself that made this proud claim. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Tyre, it is you who have said]

Tyre is using the possessive form to describe a **perfect** one that is characterized by **beauty**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I am completely beautiful]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **beauty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I am perfectly beautiful]

4.q: בְּ⁠לֵ֥ב יַמִּ֖ים גְּבוּלָ֑יִ⁠ךְ בֹּנַ֕יִ⁠ךְ כָּלְל֖וּ יָפְיֵֽ⁠ךְ
4.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if Tyre were a ship that sailed **In the heart of the seas** and that its **builders** had made beautiful. He is beginning an extended image in which he describes the city of Tyre as a magnificent trading ship. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your city lies out in the sea; those who built your city made it perfectly beautiful]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the middle of **the seas** were their **heart**. He means that Tyre was located far out in the sea. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verses 25–27. Alternate translation: [are far out in the seas]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **beauty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your builders made you perfectly beautiful]

5.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the builders of Tyre. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Tyre’s builders built all of the planks for you]
The word **Senir** is the name of a place. It is another name for Mount Hermon.

6.note: The term **ivory** describes a hard, white material that comes from the tusks and teeth of animals such as elephants, walruses, hippopotamuses, narwhals, and extinct mammoths. If your readers would not be familiar with what ivory is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [they made your deck of elephant tusks]

The word translated as **Ashurim** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that a scribe may have written the word divider in the wrong place and added the wrong vowels to the original consonants of the text, resulting in this word. With different vowels, it would say “cypresses,” which seems to fit better the meaning of this passage. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [the daughter of cypress]
The word **Kittim** is the name of a place. It probably refers to the island of Cyprus.

7.note: The term **fine linen** describes an expensive, high-quality cloth made from the flax plant, and **embroidery** describes designs sewn onto cloth with colored thread. If your readers would not be familiar with these things, you could use the names of similar things that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [Your sail was expensive cloth with colorful designs sewn on it from Egypt]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **banner** is raised high so that people can see it from far away, so the sail of Tyre could be seen from far away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [so that people could see you from far away]
The word **Elishah** is the name of a place. Its exact location is uncertain.

8.note: The word **Arvad** is the name of a city. It was on an island north of Tyre.

8.q: חֲכָמַ֤יִ⁠ךְ צוֹר֙ הָ֣יוּ בָ֔⁠ךְ הֵ֖מָּה חֹבְלָֽיִ⁠ךְ
8.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the skilled men of Tyre were the **rope-men** of a ship, the sailors who handled its ropes and steered it. He means that these wise men guided and managed the city. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your wise men, O Tyre, were in you; they were the ones who guided you]

**Rope-men** could mean: (1) regular sailors, this fits the word meaning more closely. Alternate translation: [were the men who moved the ropes to maneuver the sails] (2) pilots or helmsmen, this fits the context of **wise men** more closely. This also occurs in verses 27–29. Alternate translation: [were the men who steer the ships safely]

9.note: The word **Gebal** is the name of a city. It was on the coast north of Sidon.
The pronoun **her** refers to the city of Gebal, not to Tyre. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the wise men of Gebal]

By **the strengtheners of your cracks**, Yahweh means the people who repaired the ship by sealing the gaps in its hull so that water would not leak in. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the repairers of the gaps in your hull]

10.note: These two verses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the verses in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [In the same way, the sons of]
The words **Lud** and **Put** are the names of places. Lud was probably in Asia Minor, and Put was in northern Africa.

Yahweh is using **shield and helmet** to represent all the armor and weapons of the soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They hung all their armor and weapons in you]

The pronoun **they** refers to the men from Persia, Lud, and Put who served in Tyre’s army. The second **they** is repeated to emphasize how much those men made Tyre look splendid. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the soldiers from those nations made you splendid]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **splendor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what made you look splendid]

11.note: The phrase **and your army** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [and Helech]
The word **Gammadim** is the name of a people group. No one knows today where they lived.

The pronoun **they** refers to the men of Arvad and Tyre’s army, who guarded the walls. The second **they** is repeated to emphasize how much those men made Tyre perfected Tyre’s beauty. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the soldiers themselves perfected]
See how you translated these same phrases in verse 4. Alternate translation: [they made you perfectly beautiful]

12.note: Here, **Tarshish** represents “the merchants of Tarshish.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The merchants of Tarshish were your traders]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **abundance** and **wealth**, you could express the same ideas in another way. This also occurs in verse 18. Alternate translation: [because you had so many valuable things of every kind]

12.q: בְּ⁠כֶ֤סֶף בַּרְזֶל֙ בְּדִ֣יל וְ⁠עוֹפֶ֔רֶת נָתְנ֖וּ עִזְבוֹנָֽיִ⁠ךְ
12.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [they gave you silver, iron, tin, and lead in return for your wares]

The terms **tin** and **lead** describe soft, grayish metals that people used to make tools and other objects. If your readers would not be familiar with what tin and lead are, you could use the names of similar things that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [with silver, iron, and two kinds of soft gray metal]

13.note: The word **Javan** is the name of a people group. It refers to the Greeks.
See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 11. Alternate translation: [they indeed were your merchants]

Yahweh is using **the soul of man** to represent whole people, specifically people who were sold as slaves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with slaves]

14.note: The phrase **Beth Togarmah** is the name of a place. It was probably in the far north, in the region that is now eastern Turkey.

The term **warhorses** describes a kind of animal. This could mean: (1) horses that are trained to carry soldiers into battle. (2) horsemen, that is, men who ride horses, since the word in the original language can have that meaning. If your readers would not be familiar with what warhorses are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [horses for work and for war and mules]

15.note: Yahweh is using **The sons of Dedan** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the people of Dedan.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The descendants of Dedan] or [The people of Dedan]
The word **Dedan** is the name of a place.

Here, **your hand** represents “your control.” Yahweh means that Tyre controlled the trade with the people of **many coastlands**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you controlled the trade with the people living along many coastlands]

The term **ebony** describes a hard, dark, valuable wood. If your readers would not be familiar with what ebony is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. For ivory see verse 6). Alternate translation: [horns of ivory and valuable dark wood]

16.note: If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **abundance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from how much you produced]

16.q: בְּ֠⁠נֹפֶךְ אַרְגָּמָ֨ן וְ⁠רִקְמָ֤ה וּ⁠בוּץ֙ וְ⁠רָאמֹ֣ת וְ⁠כַדְכֹּ֔ד
16.note: The terms **emerald**, **corals**, and **ruby** describe precious stones and other valuable materials. An emerald is a green precious stone, a ruby is a red precious stone, and coral is a hard, colorful material formed in the sea. If your readers would not be familiar with these things, you could use the names of similar things that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [with green precious stones, purple, and embroidery, and fine linen, and colorful sea stones, and red precious stones]

17.note: The word **Minnith** is the name of a town. It was in the land of Ammon.

The word **pannag** is a Hebrew word which seems to describe some kind of valued food product or specialty luxury good produced in the region. Modern translations interpret it differently so if a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. Alternatively, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language.

18.note: See how you translated this same phrase in verse 16. Alternate translation: [traded with you for your abundant goods]
See how you translated this same phrase in verse 12. Alternate translation: [which you made because you were so rich]
The word **Helbon** is the name of a town. It was north of Damascus.

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **wool** that is characterized by **whiteness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and wool that is white]

19.note: The words **Vedan** and **Uzal** are the names of places. Their locations are uncertain.

The terms **cassia** and **cane** describe sweet-smelling spices made from plants. Cassia is similar to cinnamon, and cane here refers to a fragrant reed. If your readers would not be familiar with these things, you could use the names of similar things that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [wrought iron, a spice like cinnamon, and fragrant reed]

20.note: The phrase **garments of covering for riding** describes cloths that people put on the backs of animals before riding them. If your readers would not be familiar with what these garments are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [with cloths to put on animals for riding]

21.note: The pronoun **them** refers to the **lambs and rams and male goats**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [with lambs and rams and male goats, in those animals]

22.note: The word **Raamah** is the name of a place. It was probably in the southern part of Arabia.

Here, **the head of every spice** represents “the finest of all the spices.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with the best of every spice]

23.q: חָרָ֤ן וְ⁠כַנֵּה֙ וָ⁠עֶ֔דֶן רֹכְלֵ֖י שְׁבָ֑א אַשּׁ֖וּר כִּלְמַ֥ד
23.note: The words **Kanneh** and **Kilmad** are the names of places. Their locations are uncertain.

This could mean: (1) that Sheba was a separate place that traded with Tyre, along with the other places listed in this verse, as the UST indicates. (2) that **Haran and Kanneh and Eden** were **the merchants of Sheba**, meaning that they traded on behalf of Sheba. Alternate translation: [Haran and Kanneh and Eden and Sheba]

24.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the merchants from the places listed in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [These merchants from Haran, Kanneh, Eden, Sheba, Assyria, and Kilmad were your merchants]

The phrase **wrappings of blue** describes cloaks made of cloth dyed blue, and **embroidery** describes cloth decorated with designs sewn in colored thread. If your readers would not be familiar with these things, you could use the names of similar things that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [with blue-dyed cloaks and cloth decorated with colored thread]

The phrase **coverings of multicolored cloth** describes rugs or carpets woven with many colors, but no one knows today exactly what they were. If your readers would not be familiar with what these coverings are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and with colorful woven carpets tied tightly with cords]

The expressions **bound with cords** and **made firm** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is clear from the context that the merchants did it. Alternate translation: [that the merchants had bound with cords and made firm]

25.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if **The ships of Tarshish** were **travelers** or caravans that carried the goods of Tyre from place to place. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The ships of Tarshish sailed from place to place for you]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if Tyre were a ship that was **filled** with cargo and became so **heavy** that it rode low in the water. He means that Tyre became very wealthy from its trade. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And you became very wealthy through your trade across the seas]

The expression **you were filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is clear from the context that the merchants who traded with Tyre did it. Alternate translation: [And the merchants filled you with goods]

26.note: Yahweh is describing a future event as though it had already happened, to emphasize that it certainly will happen. If it would be confusing in your language to speak of this future event as if it had already happened, you could translate this in the future tense. Alternate translation: [will bring you … will shatter you]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if Tyre were a ship that **the ones rowing** it had brought out into **many waters**, that is, far out into deep water. He means that the leaders of Tyre had led the city into danger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your leaders led you into great danger]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the army that would destroy Tyre were **the wind of the east**, a strong wind that could wreck ships at sea. He is referring to the army of Babylon, which would come from the east. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the army from the east destroyed you]

27.q: הוֹנֵ⁠ךְ֙ וְ⁠עִזְבוֹנַ֔יִ⁠ךְ מַעֲרָבֵ֕⁠ךְ מַלָּחַ֖יִ⁠ךְ וְ⁠חֹבְלָ֑יִ⁠ךְ מַחֲזִיקֵ֣י בִדְקֵ֣⁠ך וְֽ⁠עֹרְבֵ֣י מַ֠עֲרָבֵ⁠ךְ וְ⁠כָל אַנְשֵׁ֨י מִלְחַמְתֵּ֜⁠ךְ אֲשֶׁר בָּ֗⁠ךְ וּ⁠בְ⁠כָל קְהָלֵ⁠ךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּ⁠תוֹכֵ֔⁠ךְ יִפְּלוּ֙ בְּ⁠לֵ֣ב יַמִּ֔ים בְּ⁠י֖וֹם מַפַּלְתֵּֽ⁠ךְ
27.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that **they will fall in the heart of the seas on the day of your fall** before the long list of people and things that will fall. Alternate translation: [On the day of your fall, all of these will fall in the heart of the seas: your wealth and your wares, your merchandise, your sailors and your rope-men, the strengtheners of your cracks and the ones exchanging your merchandise, and all of your men of war who are in you, and all of your assembly that is in your midst]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people and wealth of Tyre would sink with a ship **in the heart of the seas**. He means that they would die or be lost when Tyre was destroyed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will be lost or will die on the day when you are destroyed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fall**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the day when you are destroyed]

28.note: Yahweh says **the pasturelands will shake** as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means that the people who lived along the coast would be terrified when they heard **the cry of your rope-men**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [At the sound of the cry of your rope-men the people living along the coast will be terrified]

Here, **the pasturelands** represents “the people who live in the pasturelands along the coast.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people who live in the coastal pasturelands will shake]

29.note: Here, **the graspers of an oar** represents “the men who row ships.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And all of the rowers]

30.note: Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And they will make a lament heard over you with their voice]

30.q: וְ⁠יַעֲל֤וּ עָֽפָר֙ עַל רָ֣אשֵׁי⁠הֶ֔ם בָּ⁠אֵ֖פֶר יִתְפַּלָּֽשׁוּ
30.note: Putting dust on the head and rolling in ashes were symbolic actions by which people showed that they were very sad. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and they will put dust on their heads and roll in the ashes to show how sad they are]

31.note: Shaving the head bald and wearing sackcloth were symbolic actions by which people showed that they were mourning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And they will make themselves bald for you with a baldness, and they will gird sackcloth, to show that they are mourning for you]

Here, **make themselves bald** and **baldness** form an emphatic construction that uses a verb and a noun that come from the same root. You may be able to use a similar construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of showing the emphasis.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if grief had a **bitter** taste. He means that the sailors would feel great sorrow. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with great sorrow of soul, mourning in deep anguish]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **bitterness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [while they feel bitter in their souls]

32.q: וְ⁠קוֹנְנ֖וּ עָלָ֑יִ⁠ךְ מִ֣י כְ⁠צ֔וֹר כְּ⁠דֻמָ֖ה בְּ⁠ת֥וֹךְ הַ⁠יָּֽם
32.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and they will lament over you, asking who is like Tyre, like a silenced one in the midst of the sea]

The sailors are using the question form for emphasis. They mean that there was no other city like Tyre. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one like Tyre, like a silenced one in the midst of the sea!]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a silenced one** makes no sound, so Tyre is now silent because it has been destroyed. This could mean: (1) that Tyre is like a person whom destruction has silenced. Alternate translation: [which has been destroyed and is now as silent as a dead person in the midst of the sea] (2) that Tyre is like a ruin that lies silent **in the midst of the sea**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [which has been destroyed and is now still rocks in the midst of the sea]

33.q: בְּ⁠צֵ֤את עִזְבוֹנַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ מִ⁠יַּמִּ֔ים הִשְׂבַּ֖עַתְּ עַמִּ֣ים רַבִּ֑ים בְּ⁠רֹ֤ב הוֹנַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ וּ⁠מַ֣עֲרָבַ֔יִ⁠ךְ הֶעֱשַׁ֖רְתְּ מַלְכֵי אָֽרֶץ
33.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [When your abundant wares and merchandise went out from the seas, you greatly enriched many peoples, even the kings of the earth]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the goods that Tyre traded were food that **satisfied many peoples**. He means that Tyre supplied what many peoples needed or wanted. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you supplied what many peoples needed]

Yahweh says **the kings of the earth** as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means that Tyre made many kings in many places rich. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [you made many kings in many lands rich]

34.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if Tyre were a ship that has been **broken** apart at sea and has sunk **in the depths of waters**. He means that Tyre will be completely destroyed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [At this time you are completely destroyed, and nothing is left of you]

The expression **are broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is clear from the context that the east wind, which represents the enemy army, did it. Alternate translation: [At this time the east wind has broken you in the seas]

35.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 26:16.

Here, **shuddered a shudder** is an emphatic construction that uses a verb and a noun that come from the same root. You may be able to use a similar construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of showing the emphasis.

Yahweh is using **faces have quaked** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they looked very afraid.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have looked very afraid]

36.note: Hissing was a symbolic action by which people showed scorn and horror at something terrible that had happened to someone.
